key_findings.claim: Research on model and parameter extraction attacks against LLMs is limited and often theoretical, hindered by LLM parameter scale and confidentiality.
key_findings.context: Identified as an underexplored research gap in the future directions section.

key_findings.claim: Safe instruction tuning is a recent development that requires substantially more exploration as a defense mechanism.
key_findings.context: Highlighted as a future research direction; limited existing work on its effectiveness.

key_findings.claim: LLMs can generate functional malware in under five minutes with minimal expertise, posing a credible threat to cybersecurity.
key_findings.quantitative_result: Malware generation demonstrated in <5 minutes (Monje et al., 2023)
key_findings.context: Multiple works (GPThreats-3, RatGPT, OpwnAI) demonstrate LLM-assisted malware creation.

key_findings.claim: LLMs are vulnerable to jailbreak attacks, including automated methods (AutoDAN, GPTFuzzer, FuzzLLM) that can bypass alignment and safety training.
key_findings.context: Multiple automated jailbreaking frameworks demonstrated across aligned models including ChatGPT.

key_findings.claim: Membership inference attacks can reliably determine whether specific data was used in LLM training, posing significant privacy risks.
key_findings.context: Extensive body of work cited (Shokri et al. 2017 through Carlini et al. 2022) demonstrating progressive membership inference capabilities.

key_findings.claim: LLMs can leak personally identifiable information from training data via extraction attacks, including emails, phone numbers, and other PII.
key_findings.context: Carlini et al. (2021) demonstrated training data extraction; Huang et al. (2022) showed PII leakage from pre-trained LLMs.

key_findings.claim: LLMs exhibit measurable gender, political, and LGBTQ+ biases across multiple languages and contexts.
key_findings.context: Bias documented in reference letters, news generation, code generation, and zero-shot reasoning tasks across ChatGPT, Bard, and Bing Chat.

key_findings.claim: LLMs can be used to effectively scale spear phishing campaigns, significantly lowering the barrier for targeted attacks.
key_findings.context: Hazell (2023) and Langford & Payne (2023) demonstrate ChatGPT-assisted phishing at scale.

key_findings.claim: Backdoor (trojan) attacks on LLMs via poisoned training data or instruction tuning are feasible and can produce persistent, stealthy vulnerabilities.
key_findings.context: Multiple backdoor attack vectors covered: weight poisoning, instruction tuning poisoning, prompt-based backdoors, and RLHF poisoning.

key_findings.claim: Prompt injection attacks allow adversaries to hijack LLM-integrated applications by embedding malicious instructions in external data sources.
key_findings.context: Greshake et al. (2023) and Liu et al. (2023) demonstrate indirect prompt injection in real-world LLM-integrated apps.

key_findings.claim: Differential privacy and federated learning are viable but imperfect defenses for LLM privacy; trade-offs between privacy and utility remain unresolved.
key_findings.context: FederatedScope-LLM, FATE-LLM, and differentially private decoding frameworks discussed with acknowledged utility costs.

key_findings.claim: LLMs such as PentestGPT demonstrate measurable effectiveness as automated penetration testing assistants, enabling privilege escalation and attack chain planning.
key_findings.context: Happe et al. (2023) and Deng et al. (2023) evaluated LLMs on privilege escalation and penetration testing benchmarks.

key_findings.claim: LLM-generated text can deceive existing plagiarism detectors, with fake news detectors exhibiting systematic bias against LLM-generated content.
key_findings.context: Su et al. (2023) show detector bias; Gao et al. (2022) demonstrate ChatGPT abstracts pass plagiarism tools.

key_findings.claim: Supply chain vulnerabilities in LLM ecosystems (plugins, APIs, third-party integrations) represent an underexplored but significant attack surface.
key_findings.context: OWASP Top 10 for LLM and Iqbal et al. (2023) on ChatGPT plugin security; classified as A8 non-AI-inherent vulnerability.

llm_extraction.methods_summary: Comprehensive narrative literature review employing a structured three-category taxonomy: 'The Good' (beneficial security/privacy applications), 'The Bad' (offensive LLM applications), and 'The Ugly' (inherent LLM vulnerabilities and defenses). Papers were identified through literature search and organized into eight vulnerability subcategories (A1-A8): adversarial attacks, inference attacks, extraction attacks, bias exploitation, instruction tuning attacks, remote code execution, side-channel attacks, and supply chain vulnerabilities. Coverage spans code security, data privacy, hardware/OS/software/network/user-level attacks, and defenses including model architecture hardening, training-time defenses (differential privacy, federated learning, adversarial training), and inference-time defenses (output filtering, watermarking, prompt sanitization).
llm_extraction.limitations: The survey is a narrative review without systematic inclusion/exclusion criteria, introducing potential selection bias. The rapidly evolving LLM landscape means many cited works are preprints that have not undergone peer review. Research on model/parameter extraction attacks is acknowledged as largely theoretical due to the opacity of commercial LLM weights. The survey does not provide quantitative meta-analytic summaries or comparative benchmarks across attack/defense methods. Coverage of non-English language models and non-Western deployment contexts is limited. Safe instruction tuning and emerging jailbreak defenses are noted as insufficiently studied at time of publication (2023/early 2024).

relationships.description: Survey extends PentestGPT (Deng et al., 2023) findings by situating LLM-assisted penetration testing within a broader offensive capabilities taxonomy.
Survey synthesizes Wei et al. (2023) 'Jailbroken' findings on safety training failures alongside multiple other jailbreak works to form a comprehensive vulnerability picture.
Survey cites Carlini et al. (2022) membership inference from first principles as strong foundational evidence for LLM privacy risk claims.
AutoDAN (Liu et al., 2023) results on stealthy jailbreak generation are cited to support the finding that automated jailbreaking is a viable and scalable threat.

methodology_details.approach: Narrative literature review with structured taxonomic classification. Papers organized into three top-level categories (Good/Bad/Ugly) and eight vulnerability subcategories. Coverage includes code security, data privacy, attack vectors at hardware/OS/software/network/user levels, AI-inherent and non-AI-inherent LLM vulnerabilities, and defense strategies in model architecture, training, and inference.
methodology_details.reproducibility_notes: No formal systematic review protocol (PRISMA) reported. Search strategy and inclusion/exclusion criteria not explicitly defined. Literature primarily from 2022-2023, predominantly arXiv preprints.

domain_specific_fields.benchmark: No unified benchmark; references OWASP Top 10 for LLM as a community standard for vulnerability classification
domain_specific_fields.model_architecture: Coverage spans GPT-4, ChatGPT, Bard, LLaMA, BERT, T5, PaLM, and domain-specific fine-tuned LLMs
